title: When Instructions Multiply: Measuring and Estimating LLM Capabilities of Multiple Instructions Following

model.params_source: paper Appendix C (greedy decoding intended; the API has no top-k, the repo's --greedy flag uses temperature 0); max_tokens assumed

task.subset_rule: paper-defined: rows with exactly 5 instructions (len(instruction_id_list) == 5; 216 rows verified)
task.approximation: IFEval checkers re-implemented in the hook (strict mode, all five must pass): sentence counting by a regex splitter instead of nltk punkt, capital-word tokenization by a regex instead of nltk word_tokenize, langdetect English check skipped for the all-capital / all-lowercase instructions; the 15 instruction types present in the 216 rows are covered

items.source: github.com/kenoharada/Multiple-Instructions-Following, file data/manyifeval.jsonl (2,160 rows verified: 216 per instruction count 1-10)

prompt.source_location: Figure 1 / Table 10 (format); the complete prompts are the dataset rows

output.parse: hook parse: raw reply (IFEval checks the unstripped response)
output.parse_prose: free text checked by the IFEval rule checkers (strict mode)

metric.name: custom
metric.definition: prompt-level accuracy(n=5) = share of the 216 prompts for which all five instruction checkers pass (Eq. 1, strict)

notes: The other columns of the same row (n=1 0.94 ... n=10 0.21) can be run from the same file at 216 rows each. || [hooks_3 pass 2026-09-07] load_items keeps the 216 five-instruction rows and stores [instruction id, kwargs] pairs as the gold; score applies the checkers and returns prompt-level accuracy (Eq. 1) with per-item 0/1 for the bootstrap; failures per instruction type are printed.
